365.title: The conquerors
365.hook: emperors who conquered every land, with drums beating, also went without the Name (Savaiye)
365.howItsDone: Many Sikhs recite this among the Tav Prasad Savaiye each morning, and the nagara, the great kettledrum, is still beaten at some gurdwaras and in Sikh processions.

segments.voice: Yesterday, maate matang, and your line, they left empty-handed. Did the barefoot king lighten any wanting? And here's a small milestone: three hundred sixty-five days on this path. A whole year of days. Day three hundred sixty-five.

Before you see an army in the old world, you hear it. A low thudding comes over the hills, then another and another, until the ground itself seems to be beating. Kettledrums, war drums, the big nagaras, carried in front of the march so every village knows who's coming. The sound alone could make a city open its gates. Kings had them beaten when they set out and beaten again when they came home with a new country in their pocket. Now listen for the moment after the march has passed, when the last drumbeat rolls away down the valley. Today: the conquerors.
screen: `A THUDDING OVER THE HILLS.` → `NAGARAS IN FRONT OF THE MARCH.` → `THE LAST BEAT ROLLS AWAY.`

segments.voice: Among the ten savaiye is a verse made of that sound. In paraphrase: they went out and conquered every land in every direction, with drums and kettledrums beating. Their elephants trumpeted, their horses neighed by the thousand. Kings like these, past, present and to come, can't even be counted. And then the turn, the same turn the savaiye keep making: without remembering the Lord, at the end they all went to their final home. Another savaiya stands right beside it, about warriors in shining armor, so sure of themselves they thought even mountains couldn't move them. They too go. Here's the striking thing about the man writing it. Guru Gobind Singh had a great drum of his own. Sikh tradition remembers the Ranjit Nagara, a huge kettledrum made at Anandpur, beaten morning and evening, and its boom worried the hill kings around him. Sikhs still beat a nagara at some gurdwaras and in processions today. So this isn't someone who hated drums. He knew exactly how they sounded, and how good it felt to hear your own. What the verse is saying is simpler and harder. The sound of victory is real, and it fades. The conquerors are measured not by how far their drums carried, but by whether they remembered the One who outlasts every march. In the Sikh view, that remembering, simran, is the only thing that keeps sounding after the last beat. It's why the verse is said in the quiet of early morning, before the day's own drums start up: the deadlines, the targets, the scoreboards. They're allowed to beat. The verse just counts how long each one lasts.
screen: `THEY CONQUERED EVERY LAND.` · `WITHOUT THE NAME, THEY STILL WENT.` · `THE GURU'S OWN GREAT DRUM.` · `VICTORY IS REAL, AND IT FADES.` · then, large: `DRUMS FADE.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: let go of one small ambition. Sit and breathe slowly, and listen for a minute to whatever sounds are around you, near and far. Notice how each one rises and fades. Now find one small thing you've been pushing for that's mostly about being seen to win. More likes. The last word in an argument. Being first. Hold it lightly, like a drumbeat that's already rolling away. You don't have to give up every goal. Just set this one down, for today. If you pray, you can say Waheguru as you let it go. The bell holds the time.
The conquerors. A savaiya of kettledrums and conquered lands: kings beyond counting, who at the end still went without the Name.
Your line: drums fade. Today, when you hear a sound fade, a car passing, a song ending, a door closing, let it remind you which of your drums you can stop beating. Day three hundred sixty-five.

screen: `DAY 365 COUNTS.` → `TOMORROW: EYES SHUT LIKE A CRANE.`

pairs: the remembering that outlasts the march

tradition remembers his own great drum, the Ranjit Nagara. he knew the sound of victory, and that it fades.
the verse says the conquerors are beyond counting
kings past, present and to come can't be counted, and without the Name they all still went.
the savaiya says ambition itself is forbidden

options: your name echoes forever.
without the Name, at the end you go, like the rest.

fork.reveal: the verse lets the drums beat and the elephants trumpet, then follows the kings to their final home. without remembering the Lord, the march ends where every march ends.

trapdoor: what you thought: a verse against war.
what it means: the drums of victory are real and they fade; the conquerors are measured by whether they remembered the Lord.
what a scholar hears: the writer kept a great drum of his own, the Ranjit Nagara, so the verse speaks from inside the world of courts and campaigns, not from outside it.

366.title: Eyes shut like a crane
366.hook: what is gained by closing both eyes and sitting like a crane, pretending (Savaiye)
366.howItsDone: Many Sikhs recite this savaiya each morning as part of the Tav Prasad Savaiye, and practice simran, quiet repetition of the Name, often with eyes closed and away from any audience.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the conquerors, and your line, drums fade. Which drum did you stop beating? Today, a bird that looks very holy. Day three hundred sixty-six.

Watch a heron or a crane at the edge of a pond. It stands perfectly still on one leg, head drawn in, eyes half closed. Minutes go by. It doesn't move. If you didn't know better, you'd say it was deep in meditation, the calmest creature in the whole field. Then a fish flickers past its feet, and in a flash the beak is in the water and the fish is gone. The stillness was never peace. It was patience with an appetite. That bird became a byword long ago. Today: bak dhiaan.
screen: `A CRANE ON ONE LEG, EYES HALF SHUT.` → `IT LOOKS LIKE MEDITATION.` → `THEN THE FISH IS GONE.`

segments.voice: In Punjabi and the languages around it, there's an old name for a show-off saint: a crane devotee. Someone who looks holy while watching for the fish. Guru Gobind Singh uses that very bird in one of the savaiye. In paraphrase: what is gained by shutting both eyes and sitting like a crane in meditation? He bathed in the seven seas, and lost this world and the next. He spent his life among the things he craved, and so the days went by. The phrase in the original is bak dhiaan, crane meditation. And it doesn't laugh at stillness. Sikhs sit in stillness too, in simran, repeating the Name, and Sikhs often meditate with their eyes closed. The verse's target isn't the closed eyes. It's what's going on behind them. The crane's eyes are shut, but its mind is on the fish. So the question is turned on anyone who prays. When your eyes are closed, what are you actually watching for? Being seen as devout? Getting something? Or the One you say you're turning toward? The Guru Granth Sahib uses the same bird too, the white crane that looks spotless and is still hunting, so the image runs deep in Sikh teaching. And this verse ends on a line we'll stay with on day three hundred sixty-eight, the one the whole set leans toward. For today, the job is smaller. Stillness for show is just a crane at a pond. The verse asks for the other kind, the kind nobody sees.
screen: `THE CRANE: STILL, BUT HUNTING.` · `WHAT IS GAINED BY SHUTTING YOUR EYES?` · `NOT THE EYES, BUT WHAT'S BEHIND THEM.` · `STILLNESS NOBODY SEES.` · then, large: `NOT FOR SHOW.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: pray once with no one watching. Or, if you don't pray, sit once with no one watching. Find a spot where nobody can see you, not even a camera. Close your eyes or lower them. Breathe slowly. Notice if some part of you is still performing, sitting a bit straighter than you need to, imagining how this looks. Let that go. If you pray, you can say Waheguru once, quietly, with nobody to hear it but the One it's for. If you don't, just be still for its own sake. Nobody will ever know you did this. That's the point. The bell holds the time.
Bak dhiaan, crane meditation. Stillness that looks holy while the mind waits for the fish.
Your line: not for show. Today, do one good thing that nobody will ever find out about, and don't tell anyone, not even later. Day three hundred sixty-six.

myth: the verse says closing your eyes to meditate is wrong
Sikhs meditate with eyes closed. the verse is about what's behind the closed eyes.
a crane devotee is an old name for a show-off saint
the bird stands still and looks holy, but it's waiting for a fish.
the crane image appears only in the Dasam Granth
the Guru Granth Sahib uses the crane too, the bird that looks spotless and is still hunting.

fork.setup: you're in a room full of people at prayer. you notice you're sitting extra straight, eyes shut, hoping someone sees how still you are. what does the savaiya ask?
options: sit even stiller.
what is gained by sitting like a crane?
open your eyes and leave.
fork.reveal: the verse asks what is gained by shutting your eyes like a crane. the stillness isn't the problem. the fish you're watching for is.

original.note: Gurmukhi: bak dhiaan, crane meditation, the savaiya's picture of holiness for show.

trapdoor: what you thought: a verse against meditating with your eyes closed.
what it means: the crane's eyes are shut but its mind is on the fish. the verse asks what's behind your own closed eyes.
what a scholar hears: bak is the old word for heron or crane, and bak dhiaan, crane meditation, was a proverbial name for hypocrisy in the Guru's world.

sources.ref: Akal Ustat 29 (Tav Prasad Savaiye, the savaiya 'kahaa bhaio jo dou lochan moond kai')

367.title: Every outward ritual
367.hook: the Tenth Guru lists outward practices of many kinds and says all miss the secret without love (Savaiye)
367.howItsDone: Many Sikhs recite these verses as part of the Tav Prasad Savaiye each morning, and gurdwara teachers often apply them to Sikh practice itself, warning against rituals done without love.

segments.voice: Yesterday, bak dhiaan, and your line, not for show. Did you manage one good thing nobody found out about? Today the savaiye widen the circle. Day three hundred sixty-seven.

Make a list of everything people in one town do to be religious. Some wear something around their neck. Some keep a special object in the house. Some face a certain direction to pray. Some walk to a holy place, some fast, some give to charity, some read the same book every day for years. A poet looks at all of it, all at once, his own neighbors and his own people too, and asks one quiet question about every single practice. Not is it right. Not whose is best. Just: is the secret inside it? Today: bhed.
screen: `WHAT PEOPLE DO TO BE RELIGIOUS.` → `ALL AT ONCE, NEIGHBORS AND OWN.` → `IS THE SECRET INSIDE IT?`

segments.voice: Two of the savaiye make long lists like this. One, in paraphrase: bathing at pilgrim places, compassion, restraint, charity, vows and disciplines of many kinds; reading the scriptures of many peoples; living on air, keeping celibacy, weighing a thousand opinions. Without the Lord, the verse says, not one of these counts for anything. Another lists the outward signs of the Guru's world, things people carried, wore, faced and bowed to, the practices of the communities all around him. It ends: the whole world is tangled in false, outward rites, and no one has found the secret of the Lord. The word for secret is bhed, the hidden thing, what's actually going on inside. Now, this needs to be heard fairly. The verse names practices of the Guru's neighbors, but it isn't a list of other people's mistakes. Notice that compassion and charity are on it, things the Sikh Gurus taught constantly. So the verse can't mean they're bad. It means they're empty when they're done for their own sake, as a box to tick. And Sikh teachers are quick to turn it on Sikh habits too. Bowing to the Guru Granth Sahib without listening to it. Keeping the outward form of the faith while the heart is somewhere else. Saying the Nitnem fast, to get it done. The secret, the savaiye have been saying all week, is love. A ritual with love in it is alive. The same ritual without it is a costume.
screen: `TWO LISTS OF EVERY PRACTICE.` · `NO ONE FOUND THE SECRET, THE BHED.` · `COMPASSION IS ON THE LIST TOO.` · `TURNED ON SIKH HABITS AS WELL.` · then, large: `THE SECRET IS LOVE.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: check one habit for its heart. Sit and breathe slowly. Pick one thing you do regularly, religious or not. A prayer you say, a visit you make, a call to a parent, a donation, a family dinner. Walk through it in your mind, step by step. Then ask, gently: is there love in it right now, or has it become a box I tick? Don't judge the answer. Just see it clearly. If it's gone dry, think of one small way to put the heart back in tomorrow. If you pray, you can say Waheguru before you begin. The bell holds the time.
Bhed, the hidden thing. The savaiye's long lists of practices, and the line that says the whole world is tangled in them and hasn't found the secret.
Your line: the secret is love. Today, before you do one of your regular habits, pause for a breath and put the heart back in it on purpose. Day three hundred sixty-seven.

screen: `DAY 367 COUNTS.` → `TOMORROW: THOSE WHO LOVED FOUND HIM.`

368.title: Those who loved found Him
368.hook: I tell the truth, listen all: those who loved found the Lord (Savaiye)
368.howItsDone: Many Sikhs recite this savaiya each morning as part of the Tav Prasad Savaiye, and its closing line is widely quoted and sung in kirtan as a summary of the Sikh teaching on love.

segments.voice: Yesterday, bhed, and your line, the secret is love. Did one habit get its heart back? Today, the line the savaiye have been leaning toward. Day three hundred sixty-eight.

You've been in a room like this. A family dinner, a meeting, a wedding speech that's gone on a bit. People are half-listening, checking phones. Then someone stands up and says: I'm going to tell you the truth now. Everyone listen. And the room goes quiet, because that's not a sentence you say lightly. It means everything up to now was warm-up. One of the savaiye has exactly that sentence in it, after all the elephants and conquerors and cranes, and what comes after it is the line this whole week has been leaning toward. Today: prem.
screen: `I'M GOING TO TELL YOU THE TRUTH.` → `EVERYONE LISTEN.` → `THE ROOM GOES QUIET.`

segments.voice: Here it is in the original, transliterated: saach kahoon sun leho sabhai, jin prem kio tin hee prabh paaio. Take it in pieces. Saach kahoon: I speak the truth. Sun leho sabhai: listen, all of you. Then, jin prem kio: those who loved. Tin hee prabh paaio: they alone found the Lord. Two little details make this line. First, hee, that small word. Not those who loved also found Him, among others. Only they. After all the parades, the ascetics and the drums and the rituals, there's one road left standing. Second, the tense. Found. It's past tense. The verse doesn't speak like a theory about how someone might reach God. It speaks like a witness reporting what has already happened. Those who loved, found. Now, what kind of love? Sikhs hear it as prem, a whole-hearted longing for the One, the kind that changes how you live. Guru Nanak has a saying in the Guru Granth Sahib that helps here. In paraphrase: if you want to play this game of love, come to my lane with your head in your hand. So it isn't a soft feeling. It costs. Sikh tradition remembers many who loved that way, all the way. But the Gurus also show that love starts small: in seva, in langar, in the way you treat the person in front of you. You can't love God, Sikhs often say, and be careless with the people God made. It fits that the line closes the crane verse. You can fake stillness. You can fake ritual. Love is the one thing that doesn't work as a performance.
screen: `I SPEAK THE TRUTH. LISTEN, ALL.` · `ONLY THOSE WHO LOVED.` · `FOUND: IT ALREADY HAPPENED.` · `LOVE THAT COSTS, AND STARTS SMALL.` · then, large: `THOSE WHO LOVED, FOUND.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: tell someone you love them. Sit for a moment first and breathe. Let a face come to mind, someone you love but haven't said it to lately. A parent, a sibling, a friend, a grandparent, a partner. Picture them clearly. Notice what you actually love about them, one specific thing. Then, when the bell ends, send them a message or call them, and say it plainly, with that one thing in it. It might feel awkward. That's fine. Love that costs a little awkwardness is still love. If you pray, you can hold them in Waheguru first. The bell holds the time.
Prem, whole-hearted love. Jin prem kio tin hee prabh paaio: those who loved, they alone found the Lord. The line the savaiye lean toward.
Your line: those who loved, found. Today, find one moment to love someone out loud, in words or in an act, and let it cost you something small. Day three hundred sixty-eight.

fork.reveal: jin prem kio tin hee prabh paaio: those who loved, they alone found the Lord. the line closes the crane savaiya and sums up all ten.

trapdoor: what you thought: a nice line about love.
what it means: after every outward road falls away, only those who loved found the Lord. past tense, a report.
what a scholar hears: the emphatic hee, only, and the past tense paaio, found, turn the line from advice into testimony.

369.title: Savaiye close
369.hook: the ten verses sharpen one point: love, not display
369.howItsDone: Many Sikhs recite all ten Tav Prasad Savaiye each morning after Jaap Sahib; they are also read while amrit is prepared at the Khalsa initiation, where initiates take on the five articles of faith.

segments.voice: Yesterday, prem, the line at the heart of the savaiye, and yours: those who loved, found. Did you love someone out loud? Today we close the ten verses. Day three hundred sixty-nine.

Here's a strange thing about the man who wrote the ten savaiye. Guru Gobind Singh is the Guru who gave the Khalsa its outward form. The five articles that Sikhs who take amrit keep on their bodies every day: uncut hair, a comb, a steel bracelet, cotton undershorts, the kirpan. He shaped how a whole community looks, to this day. And the same Guru wrote ten verses saying outward forms, without love, aren't worth a single seed. Is that a contradiction? Sikh teachers have an answer, and it's a good way to close these ten verses. Today: savaiye.
screen: `THE GURU WHO GAVE THE KHALSA ITS FORM.` → `WROTE THAT FORM WITHOUT LOVE IS NOTHING.` → `A CONTRADICTION?`

segments.voice: Start by laying the ten verses side by side. They make the same move every time. Set up something impressive, then weigh it. Tav prasad, cupped hands, waiting, over the door. The ascetics of every order, weighed: not one ratti without love. Maate matang: their kings left barefoot. The conquerors with their drums: the beat faded. The crane with its eyes shut: still, and hunting. Bhed, compassion and charity included: the secret missed. And then the line the set leans on: those who loved, they alone found the Lord. Ten verses, one point, sharpened until it cuts. Love, not display. Now the question from the hook. Sikhs don't hear the savaiye as saying the outward form doesn't matter. The same verses are recited while the amrit is prepared, at the very ceremony where people take on the five articles. So the form and the warning are given in the same breath, on purpose. As some Sikh teachers put it, the form is meant to carry the love, the way a cup carries water. A beautiful cup that's empty is still empty. But nobody throws away the cup because of that. They fill it. The danger the savaiye name is the cup admired for itself: the turban worn for show, the bani rushed to be done, the kirpan as a costume. And the savaiye don't let anyone off: not kings, not yogis, not pilgrims. Many readers hear the warning reaching the Khalsa too, since these same verses are said at its own initiation.
screen: `TEN VERSES, ONE MOVE: WEIGH IT.` · `LOVE, NOT DISPLAY.` · `SAID AS THE AMRIT IS PREPARED.` · `THE FORM IS A CUP FOR THE LOVE.` · then, large: `LOVE, NOT DISPLAY.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: read your favorite one again. Settle and breathe. Think back over this week's verses: the ascetics, the elephants, the conquerors, the crane, the rituals, the line about love. Which one stayed with you? If you have the text or a recording, go to it and read or listen to that one savaiya again, slowly. If you don't, just replay its picture in your mind. Then ask what it was about that one that caught you. If you pray, you can say Waheguru when you've finished. The bell holds the time.
Savaiye, four-line verses. Ten of them weigh the ascetics, the elephants, the conquerors, the crane and every ritual, and find only love was ever heavy enough.
Your line: love, not display. Today, look at one thing you wear or keep that means something to you, and ask whether it's carrying love or just being admired. Day three hundred sixty-nine.

370.title: A prayer for protection
370.hook: the Tenth Guru's quiet prayer asking to be sheltered
370.howItsDone: Many Sikhs recite Chaupai Sahib every morning as part of the Nitnem and again within the evening Rehras, and many also say it before travel, at night, or in times of fear.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the ten savaiye closed, and your line was love, not display. Did something you wear or keep carry love today? Now a new bani begins, and it's a quieter one. Day three hundred seventy.

Some prayers are made for a crowd. They're big and public, and sung by a whole hall at once. Others are made for one person, very quietly. The kind you say under your breath in the car on the way to the hospital. Or at three in the morning when the house makes a noise. Or on a plane when the wheels leave the ground. The Tenth Guru, who wrote war poetry and praise as wide as the sky, also wrote one of those. A small, close prayer. Its own heading calls it a request. Today: a prayer for protection.
screen: `PRAYERS MADE FOR A CROWD.` → `AND PRAYERS UNDER YOUR BREATH.` → `THE TENTH GURU WROTE ONE.`

segments.voice: Today's word is Benti Chaupai. Benti means a humble request, the kind you make to someone greater than you, standing at their door. Chaupai is the meter, verses whose lines fall into four parts. Its heading in the Dasam Granth reads, roughly, the poet speaks: a request, in chaupai. And it's short enough to learn by heart, which many Sikhs do. It's one of the five banis of the Sikh morning, it's in the evening Rehras, and it's recited while the amrit is prepared. One honest note: Sikhs don't all stop it in the same place. Some traditions recite a longer version, some a shorter one, with a few extra verses at the end. Both are said with devotion, and this path follows the common pattern without ranking either. The prayer opens with four lines, and you can hear its whole shape in them. In paraphrase: protect me, giving me your hand. May the wish of my heart be fulfilled. May my mind stay at your feet. Take me as your own, and look after me. Notice what isn't there. No list of demands. No bargaining. No I'll do this if you do that. Just a hand, a heart, feet, and belonging. Over the next ten days we'll take those lines and the ones after them one at a time. And notice who is praying: a Guru who led his people through years of war. Sikhs don't hear Chaupai as a frightened prayer. They hear it as the request of someone who knew that being brave is not the same as being alone.
screen: `BENTI: A HUMBLE REQUEST.` · `CHAUPAI: LINES IN FOUR PARTS.` · `MORNING, EVENING, AND AT AMRIT.` · `HAND, HEART, FEET, BELONGING.` · then, large: `SHELTER ME.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: read the first four lines. If you can, look up Chaupai Sahib in Gurmukhi or transliteration and read just the opening four lines aloud, slowly, even if you stumble on the sounds. If you can't, sit with the four ideas instead, one breath each. A hand. A heart's wish. Resting at the feet. Being taken as someone's own. Breathe in with each one and let it settle. If you pray, you can say Waheguru after the fourth. If you don't, just notice which of the four you most needed today. The bell holds the time.
Benti Chaupai. A humble request in four-part verse: the Tenth Guru's short prayer for shelter, said morning and evening and at the amrit ceremony.
Your line: shelter me. Today, when something makes you uneasy, a phone call, a bad headline, a long drive, let those two words rise up, and notice what changes. Day three hundred seventy.

371.title: Protect me with your hand
371.hook: hamree karo hath dai rachhaa: give me Your hand and keep me safe (Chaupai)
371.howItsDone: Many Sikhs recite this opening line of Chaupai Sahib each morning and evening, and some say it on its own as a short prayer before a journey or a difficult moment.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Benti Chaupai, and your line, shelter me. This week: the drums faded, the crane was found out, the secret was love, those who loved found, the ten savaiye closed, and a quiet prayer began. Today, its first line. Day three hundred seventy-one.

In Punjabi, there's an old way of saying I'll stand by you: I've taken your arm. Someone who takes another person's arm is making a promise, the kind you don't walk away from. It's what a family does for a newcomer, what an elder does for a frightened child, what a friend does when your life falls apart. It's not a handshake. It's a grip. And it's the first picture in the Tenth Guru's prayer for protection, the very first thing it asks for, before anything else. Today: rachhaa.
screen: `I'VE TAKEN YOUR ARM.` → `NOT A HANDSHAKE. A GRIP.` → `THE PRAYER'S FIRST PICTURE.`

segments.voice: The line, transliterated, is hamree karo haath dai rachhaa. Take it apart. Hamree: mine, our. Karo: make, do. Haath dai: giving your hand. Rachhaa: protection, guarding. Protect me, giving me your hand. Rachhaa is the poem's form of raksha, protection, the word also used for protective threads and amulets. But notice what the line asks for instead of a thread or an amulet. A hand. Not an object to carry around, but the protector themselves, reaching in. The Guru isn't asking for a charm. He's asking to be held. Sikh teaching often points away from charms like these and toward the One, directly. Now, why a hand? Because a hand is personal. An army can protect you. A wall can protect you. But only someone who is right there, close enough to touch, can give you their hand. The line asks God to be that near. And it asks it of someone who sees everything, as later lines will say, so it isn't a request for God to notice. It's a request to be held, while noticed. And this same prayer ends, near its close, with that Punjabi picture from the hook: the one who has taken my arm. We'll get there on day three hundred seventy-eight. For now, just the first line. Hamree karo haath dai rachhaa. Keep me by the hand.

segments.voice: Here's the practice: rest your hand on your heart. Sit comfortably and place one hand flat on the center of your chest. Feel its warmth, its weight. Feel the heartbeat underneath, or just the rise and fall of breathing. Stay like that and let the hand do what a hand does: steady you. Breathe slowly. If you pray, you can say the line, hamree karo haath dai rachhaa, or simply Waheguru, under your breath. If you don't, just let yourself be held for a minute, even if it's your own hand doing the holding. The bell holds the time.
Rachhaa, protection. Hamree karo haath dai rachhaa: the first line of Chaupai, asking not for a charm but for a hand, someone near enough to hold you.
Your line: keep me by the hand. Today, offer someone your hand, literally or not: a steadying arm, a lift, help with something heavy. Day three hundred seventy-one.
